1051.title: Renewal
1051.hook: temples rebuilt, texts reprinted, ordinations renewed
1051.howItsDone: Buddhist communities rebuild damaged temples, reprint and recopy scriptures, and, where a line of ordination has lapsed, invite monastics from other countries to give ordination again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, temples built by families far from home, from rented rooms to shrine rooms in houses. Your line: a home far from home. Did you learn a new name? Day one thousand fifty-one.

On a mountain in Korea, at a temple called Haeinsa, long halls hold row after row of carved wooden blocks. Each block is a page of scripture, cut in reverse so it can be inked and printed. The story the temple tells is that these blocks are themselves a second try: an earlier set was lost to fire in a time of war, and monks and carvers sat down and made the whole thing again, block by block. Today isn't about a loss. It's about what people do after one.
screen: `ROW AFTER ROW OF WOODEN BLOCKS.` → `A SECOND TRY, BLOCK BY BLOCK.` → `WHAT PEOPLE DO AFTER A LOSS.`

segments.voice: Renewal comes in three kinds today. Temples rebuilt. You've met them through this whole stretch: in Cambodia, Mongolia, China, and in exile in India, communities came back to ruined or empty halls and opened the doors again. Texts reprinted. The carved blocks at Haeinsa are one picture of it: when a set of scriptures is lost, someone sits down and makes it again. And ordinations renewed. You met the rule behind this one in Cambodia: a monk can't ordain himself. Full ordination needs a gathering of monks who were fully ordained themselves, in a line that runs back, by tradition, to the Buddha. If that line dies out in a country, nobody there can give it. Sri Lankan histories tell of a time when that happened, and of monks invited from Siam, today's Thailand, who came and gave ordination again. One branch of Sri Lanka's sangha still carries Siam's name. Underneath all of this sits a teaching the tradition never hid. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Buddha's last words, which this block first heard on the day about persecutions, are, in Rhys Davids's translation: "Behold now, brethren, I exhort you, saying, 'Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!'" Decay is expected. Temples, printing blocks, lines of teachers are all component things. Read this way, a loss isn't a sign that the teaching was false. It's the moment to work with diligence. Carve again. Invite again. Open the doors again.
screen: `TEMPLES REBUILT.` · `TEXTS CARVED AND PRINTED AGAIN.` · `ORDINATION INVITED BACK FROM SIAM.` · then, large: `DECAY IS INHERENT IN ALL COMPONENT THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: rebuild one small thing. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind something small that's broken or lapsed in your life. A habit you dropped. A friendship that went quiet. A chair with a loose leg. A practice that slipped. Don't scold yourself about it. Just look at it, the way the carvers looked at a blank block of wood. Ask one question: what's the first small cut? A message. A screwdriver. Five minutes tomorrow morning. Hold that first step in mind and breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Renewal. Temples rebuilt, texts carved again, ordination invited back: the tradition expects decay, and answers it with diligence. Today's word.
Your line: it renews. Today, take the first small step on the thing you chose: send the message, fix the leg, sit for five minutes. Then let it be enough for today. Day one thousand fifty-one.

1052.title: History, closed
1052.hook: the tradition has been broken and has healed, many times
1052.howItsDone: Buddhist communities remember hard histories in memorial services, rebuilt temples and teachings on impermanence, and some dedicate merit or loving-kindness to those who carried the tradition through loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday, carved blocks made again and ordination invited back from Siam. Your line: it renews. Did you take the first small step? Today closes this stretch of history. Day one thousand fifty-two.

Why spend so many days on hard history in a daily practice? That was the question this block began with, and the answer then was simple: the tradition is made of people, and people fail and endure. Since then you've heard about kings and monks, closed monasteries, wars, exile, killing years, empty niches in a cliff, and broken trust. You've also heard about rebuilding, apology, dignity, chaplains and temples far from home. Today we close the history, and hold all of it at once.
screen: `MADE OF PEOPLE.` → `FAILING AND ENDURING.` → `HOLD ALL OF IT AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape of what we've walked through. First, the breaks from outside. Rulers protected the sangha and used it. Monasteries were closed by governments. Communities were scattered into exile, or nearly destroyed. Second, the harms from inside. Some Buddhist institutions backed wars. Some monks spoke for hate, while others spoke against it. Some teachers abused the trust placed in them. This block didn't pretend the tradition only ever suffered things; sometimes its own people did the harm. Third, the healing. Monasteries rebuilt in India with their old names. A sangha in Cambodia raised again from very few. Doors in China and Mongolia opened again. Apologies made. Dignity claimed in India by people once called untouchable. Ordination invited back across the sea. And fourth, the reason none of this surprises the tradition itself: anicca, impermanence. Everything made comes apart, including institutions. The teaching doesn't ask anyone to pretend otherwise. What it offers is a way to stand while things come apart. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in a picture: "By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm." History has been a flood more than once. Again and again, people have built islands in it: a practice kept, a text carried, a door opened. Broken, and healed, and broken again. That's the history this path has been telling.
screen: `THE BREAKS FROM OUTSIDE.` · `THE HARMS FROM INSIDE.` · `THE HEALING, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · then, large: `AN ISLAND WHICH NO FLOOD CAN OVERWHELM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: sit with gratitude. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind the people who carried this tradition through the hard years. Monks walking over mountains. A nun hiding a text. A grandmother in Phnom Penh who still remembered the chants. Carvers bent over wooden blocks. You don't need names. With each breath, let a little thanks go toward them. If your mind drifts to the harms, let them be there too. Gratitude doesn't erase them. It just stands next to them. The bell holds the time.
History. The long story of a tradition broken from outside and from within, and healed, many times, by people who rebuilt, carried and opened doors again. Today's word.
Your line: broken and healed. Tomorrow the festival year begins again. Today, thank one person, living or remembered, who helped put something in your life back together. Day one thousand fifty-two.

1053.title: Vesak, the third time
1053.hook: a third Vesak: what has changed in you since the first
1053.howItsDone: On Vesak, Buddhists in Theravada lands visit temples, keep extra precepts, give food and light lamps and lanterns to remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the history: a tradition broken from outside and within, and healed again and again. Your line: broken and healed. Whom did you thank? Today, the festival year begins. Day one thousand fifty-three.

A small clay lamp, a wick, a little oil. That's all it takes. On Vesak night, in Sri Lanka and other Theravada lands, lamps like that line windowsills and temple walls, and paper lanterns hang over the streets. You've been here twice before on this path. In your first year, Vesak arrived as a new word. In your second, you went deeper into Colombo's lanterns and the eight precepts. Now a third Vesak comes round, and a third lamp. Same moon. Same story. The question today is about the one holding the lamp.
screen: `A CLAY LAMP, A WICK, A LITTLE OIL.` → `THE SAME MOON, A THIRD TIME.` → `WHO HOLDS THE LAMP?`

segments.voice: First, the day itself, briefly. In Theravada lands, Vesak remembers the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his passing away, all on the full moon of the month of Vesakha. People visit temples, keep extra precepts, give food, and light lamps. Second, why lamps. This path heard the line once already, when the stretch on teachers closed. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, near the end of his life, the Buddha tells Ananda not to look for some outside refuge. In Rhys Davids's translation: "Therefore, O Ânanda, be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves." A lamp on Vesak night honors the Buddha, and it also points back at the one who lights it. Third, a quiet surprise in that line. The Pali word behind lamp is dipa, and dipa can also mean island. Some translators write be lamps unto yourselves; others write be islands unto yourselves. Both pictures work. A lamp gives light in the dark. An island stands firm in a flood, like the island from yesterday's Dhammapada line. Fourth, the third time. A festival that comes back each year works a little like a mirror on a wall you pass. The mirror doesn't change. The one passing it may. Three Vesaks on this path is not a test, and there's no right answer to what it shows. Some people notice they know more. Some notice they need less. Some notice nothing much, and that's honest too. The Dhammapada asks, in Müller's words: "Why do you not seek a light, ye who are surrounded by darkness?" Tonight's lamp is a small, plain answer.
screen: `BORN, AWAKE, GONE, ONE FULL MOON.` · `BE YE LAMPS UNTO YOURSELVES.` · `DIPA: A LAMP, OR AN ISLAND.` · then, large: `THE SAME MOON. YOU, A THIRD TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: light a lamp. If you have a candle or a small light, light it now, safely. If not, picture one. Sit, and watch the flame for a few breaths. Then, gently, ask: what's different since I first heard the word Vesak on this path? Don't hunt for a big answer. Let whatever comes, come. A habit. A question. A name. Nothing at all. Just keep the flame in view and let the breath be slow. The bell holds the time.
Vesak. The full moon when Theravada Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, and light lamps, a little light for each of us to carry. Today's word.
Your line: the third lamp. Tonight, before you sleep, turn every light off but one, and sit with that one for a minute before you switch it off. Day one thousand fifty-three.

1054.title: Flower festival
1054.hook: Hanamatsuri in Japan: flowers and sweet tea for the baby Buddha
1054.howItsDone: At Hanamatsuri, temples in Japan set up a small flower-covered shrine with a statue of the newborn Buddha, and visitors ladle sweet tea over it, and some take tea home to drink.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a third Vesak, and the Buddha's words to Ananda: be lamps unto yourselves. Your line: the third lamp. Did you sit with one light? Day one thousand fifty-four.

You've stood in this courtyard before. In your first year on this path, Hanamatsuri arrived as a new word: a tiny roofed shrine covered in fresh flowers, a little statue of the baby Buddha, one hand pointing up and one pointing down, and a line of children ladling sweet tea over his head. The flowers and the tea come back every spring. This time, look past the scene to the old text behind it, and to the quiet turn at its very end, which is easy to miss.
screen: `THE FLOWER SHRINE, AGAIN.` → `ONE HAND UP, ONE HAND DOWN.` → `A QUIET TURN IN AN OLD TEXT.`

segments.voice: The birth story the festival acts out comes from a sutta in the Majjhima Nikaya, the one on wonderful and marvelous qualities. Its setting is easy to skip. Monks are sitting together after their meal, marveling at the Buddha's powers, when he walks in and asks what they were talking about. He asks Ananda to say more, and Ananda recites a long list of wonders he says he heard from the Buddha's own lips. The mother gives birth standing. The newborn stands on his own feet, takes seven steps, looks around, and declares that he is foremost in the world and that this is his last birth. Two streams of water, one cool and one warm, appear from the sky to bathe mother and child. That's the wonder the ladles repeat, and the flowers stand for the garden at Lumbini, where tradition places the birth. Now the turn. When Ananda finishes, the Buddha doesn't add a louder miracle. In paraphrase, he says: then remember this too as wonderful. For the one who has woken up, feelings are known as they arise, as they stay, and as they pass away. So are perceptions. So are thoughts. After all the marvels of the birth, the sutta ends on the plainest one: seeing clearly what is happening in one's own mind. That changes how the festival can look. The baby with one hand raised is where the story starts. A child's full attention on a ladle and a thin stream of tea is closer to where the sutta ends.
screen: `MONKS MARVELING AFTER THE MEAL.` · `ANANDA'S LIST OF BIRTH WONDERS.` · `TWO STREAMS OF WATER, COOL AND WARM.` · then, large: `FEELINGS KNOWN AS THEY ARISE AND PASS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: pour gently. If you have a cup of tea or water nearby, hold it. If not, picture one. Sit, and let the breath settle. Slowly, with full attention, pour a little water: over a plant, into a glass, into your own palm. Notice the sound, the weight, the way it moves. Pour as if over something new and fragile. Then set the cup down and rest your hands. Breathe, and stay a moment with how careful that was. The bell holds the time.
Flower festival. Hanamatsuri, when temples in Japan cover a small shrine in flowers and people pour sweet tea over the baby Buddha, remembering his birth in the garden. Today's word.
Your line: sweet tea. Today, make one cup of something for someone else, and pour it slowly, the way the children pour over the baby Buddha. Day one thousand fifty-four.

1055.title: Asalha again
1055.hook: the first sermon, heard a third year
1055.howItsDone: On Asalha Puja, Theravada Buddhists visit temples to hear the first sermon recited or explained, make offerings, and in some places walk around the temple with candles; the rains retreat begins soon after.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a flower shrine and children ladling sweet tea over the baby Buddha. Your line: sweet tea. Did you pour a cup slowly for someone? Day one thousand fifty-five.

Five wandering ascetics are camped in the Deer Park near Benares. They used to practice with Gotama, and then he gave up the harsh fasting, and they left him in disgust. Now one of them spots a familiar figure walking up the path. It's him. The Vinaya tells us they make a pact on the spot: we won't stand up for him, we won't take his bowl, we'll just leave a seat out in case he wants to sit. He keeps walking toward them. Today, for the Asalha full moon, we hear what happened next, a third time.
screen: `FIVE ASCETICS IN THE DEER PARK.` → `WE WON'T STAND UP FOR HIM.` → `HE KEEPS WALKING TOWARD THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the pact breaks. As he comes closer, the Vinaya says, they can't keep it. One takes his bowl and robe, one sets out a seat, one brings water for his feet. The text says simply that they were not able to keep it. Second, the middle way. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the Setting in Motion of the Wheel of the Teaching, opens with two extremes, in paraphrase: a life given over to sense pleasure, which is low and unprofitable, and a life given over to self-torment, which is painful and unprofitable. He had tried both. Between them runs a middle way. Third, the four truths, the heart of the sermon. There is suffering: birth, aging, sickness, death, being with what you don't love, losing what you do. Suffering has a cause: craving, the thirst that keeps reaching. Suffering can end, when that craving fades and is let go. And there's a way to that ending, the noble eightfold path. Fourth, the listener who heard it. The sutta says that as the Buddha spoke, one of the five, Kondanna, saw it clearly, and the sutta gives what he saw: whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease. Some readers hear that short line as the whole sermon folded small. So why hear it a third time? Because the sutta isn't only an event in a park. In the Theravada tradition, the Asalha full moon keeps it alive every year, and the wheel is said to have been set rolling, not finished. It turns again each time someone hears it.
screen: `THE PACT BREAKS.` · `TWO EXTREMES, ONE MIDDLE WAY.` · `FOUR TRUTHS.` · then, large: `WHATEVER ARISES, CEASES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: say the four truths from memory. Sit, and settle the breath. Then, slowly, say them, inwardly or in a low voice. There is suffering. Suffering has a cause, craving. Suffering can end. There is a path to its ending. If one slips from memory, that's fine; start again. Say them once more, and between each one, take a full breath and let the words sink. Then rest in the quiet after the last one. The bell holds the time.
Asalha again. The full moon when Theravada Buddhists remember the first sermon in the Deer Park: the middle way, the four truths, and the wheel set rolling. Today's word.

Your line: the wheel, again. Today, notice one craving as it rises, a snack, a scroll, a last word, and watch it fade on its own, the way Kondanna saw: whatever arises, ceases. Day one thousand fifty-five.

1056.title: The Bon dance
1056.hook: Bon Odori: circle dances at Obon to welcome and send off the ancestors
1056.howItsDone: During Obon, communities in Japan and Japanese communities abroad hold Bon Odori, circle dances around a lantern-hung tower with drums, open to anyone, as ancestors are welcomed home and later sent off with fires and lanterns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asalha again: the Deer Park, a broken pact, and the four truths a third time. Your line: the wheel, again. Did you watch one craving fade? Day one thousand fifty-six.

A summer evening in Japan. In a schoolyard or a temple courtyard stands a wooden tower, hung with paper lanterns, and up on top someone is beating a big drum. Around the tower, a ring of people moves slowly, all doing the same simple steps: a clap, a turn, hands lifted and lowered. Grandparents in light cotton robes. Teenagers. Little kids copying whoever is in front of them. Anyone can step in. This is Bon Odori, the Bon dance, and the ones it's danced for are not in the circle.
screen: `A TOWER HUNG WITH LANTERNS.` → `A RING OF PEOPLE, THE SAME STEPS.` → `DANCING FOR THE UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: First, the festival around the dance. Obon, met on this path last year, is the summer time in Japan when families welcome their ancestors home. Some families light a small fire at the door to guide them in, and at the end, fires and floating lanterns send them off again. The dance happens in between, while the ancestors are thought of as guests. Second, the old story beneath it. The Ullambana Sutra, a Chinese Buddhist scripture, tells of Moggallana, who uses his powers to find his dead mother suffering among the hungry ghosts, and finds that the food he brings her can't reach her. The Buddha tells him that offerings to the gathered monks at the end of the rains retreat can bring relief to parents and ancestors, and through that offering his mother is freed. Third, a story people tell. In Japan, a popular story says that Moggallana danced for joy when his mother was released, and that the Bon dance remembers his joy. That detail isn't in the sutra; it's a story told about it, and it's honest to say so. Fourth, why a circle. A circle has no front row and no audience. Nobody has to be good at it. The steps repeat until feet know them without thinking. The living move together, for the dead, and for one another. An old teaching sits close by. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha says parents can't easily be repaid, not even by carrying your mother on one shoulder and your father on the other for a hundred years. The sutta's own answer is to help them toward faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom. A Bon dance is a different kind of remembering: a few steps, a clap, a turn, done together.
screen: `WELCOMED HOME, THEN SENT OFF.` · `MOGGALLANA AND HIS MOTHER.` · `HE DANCED FOR JOY, PEOPLE SAY.` · then, large: `A CIRCLE HAS NO AUDIENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: move to music for a minute. Put on a song you love, or one someone you've lost used to love, or just hum. Stand if you can, or stay seated. Sway. Lift your hands and lower them. Clap once, softly, if you like. Keep the steps simple, the same ones over and over. If someone comes to mind, let them be in the room with you while you move. When the minute is done, sit, and let your heart and breath slow down again. The bell holds the time.
The Bon dance. Bon Odori, the circle dance of Obon in Japan, where the living move together to welcome the ancestors home and send them off again. Today's word.

Your line: dance for them. Today, when a song comes on that someone you've lost would have loved, let your body move a little, even just a tapping foot, and let it be for them. Day one thousand fifty-six.

1057.title: Kathina again
1057.hook: the robe offering at the end of the rains
1057.howItsDone: In Theravada countries, lay people offer robe cloth and other useful things to monasteries at Kathina ceremonies after the rains retreat ends, and the monks receive the cloth as a community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bon dance: circles of people moving together at Obon to welcome the ancestors home and send them off again. Your line: dance for them. Who did you move for? Day one thousand fifty-seven.

Every day, through heat and rain, a monk's robe is worn, slept in, washed, mended, and washed again, until it wears out. A monk owns very few things, so the robe is close to everything he has. At the end of the rains retreat, lay people in Theravada countries bring cloth for new robes, at a ceremony called Kathina. This is the third year you've met it. The first time, it was the story of how the offering began. The second, the weaving that runs through the night. Today, the robe itself: how it is sewn, and where it goes after it is given.

segments.voice: Start with the pattern. In the Vinaya, the monastic rulebook, the Buddha is walking through the country of Magadha and looks out over the rice fields, laid out in strips with low banks between them. He turns to Ananda and asks whether he could make robes for the monks like that. Ananda can, and does. So the robe is not one smooth length of cloth. It is sewn from cut pieces, set out like fields with borders running between them. The text gives a reason: cloth cut into pieces suits someone who has left home, and nobody would want to steal it. Now follow the robe to its end. Another story in the Vinaya comes after the Buddha has died. The women of King Udena's palace give Ananda a great gift of robes, and the king, puzzled, asks him what he will do with so many. Ananda says he'll give them to monks whose robes are worn thin. And the old robes? They become coverlets. The old coverlets? Mattress covers. The old mattress covers? Rugs for the floor. The old rugs? Cloths for wiping feet. The old foot cloths? Dusters. And the old dusters? Torn into shreds, beaten into clay, and spread as plaster on the floor. Nothing is wasted. That is what the Kathina cloth walks into. It is not a keepsake for a shelf. It becomes a robe that is worn every day, then passed down the line of uses until the last scrap is part of the floor underfoot. That is the shape of the gift: useful, and meant to be used up.
screen: `THE PATTERN OF THE RICE FIELDS.` · `CUT PIECES, SEWN WITH BORDERS.` · `ANANDA ANSWERS THE KING.` · then, large: `USED DOWN TO THE PLASTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: give something useful. Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one useful thing you could give: a warm coat you never wear, a good pan, a tool, an hour of help. Not something precious to admire. Something that will get worn. See it in someone else's hands, being used, getting scuffed, wearing thin. Let that be the whole gift, with no say in how it's used and no thank you needed. If you decide to give it, notice how that feels. The bell holds the time.
Kathina again. The cloth offered at the end of the rains, sewn into a robe laid out like rice fields, and used until nothing is left. Today's word.
Your line: the robe given. Today, give one useful thing, something that will be worn out rather than kept, and let it go where it's needed. Day one thousand fifty-seven.
